input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "please help me shape a prompt for a practical internal guide for the north quay rehearsal archive. it should ask for a guide that explains how staff and volunteers handle rehearsal recordings from arrival through a decision about access, not a history of the archive and not a broad policy or legal document. the archive is a small nonprofit collection in a converted community hall, with recordings from local theatre and dance groups between 2014 and 2022. there are about 640 sessions, mostly WAV audio, with a smaller number of MP3s and a few rehearsal videos. The archive has a desktop computer called Rowan at the intake desk and a separate backup drive named Birch. The paper logs stay in folders by year, and staff currently note an intake date and a box or shelf location on each log. The guide can suggest a consistent order for these steps, but should not propose buying new equipment or software.

1. Please cover these parts in a usable sequence, and make sure the steps distinguish what staff check from what they record:

   - copy digital files to Rowan and Birch, then verify the copied files against the source using the archive's checksum tool;

The guide should not treat a file that opens as automatically cleared for public listening. The archive uses checksum verification to check that a copy matches its source, not to determine consent or sound quality. Don't suggest that a paper log provides details that were never written on it.

For the copying step, make the action conditional and show both branches clearly. If the checksum matches the source, keep the source file unchanged and retain the verified copies on Rowan and Birch. If the checksum does not match, do not replace or overwrite the source; set the suspect copy aside and notify the archive coordinator before anyone tries another copy. The guide should make clear that the mismatch branch applies to the affected file, rather than implying every file in the box failed. The coordinator's next decision is outside the requested guide, so don't invent what happens after notification. Please keep this rule visible again when describing how a volunteer closes an intake shift, so it still matters after the first copying steps.

Access needs its own part, separate from the file checks. Some groups gave permission for staff-only preservation but have not agreed to public listening. Other groups signed a consent sheet allowing public access to selected sessions, and the sheet may name specific tracks or set-list items rather than an entire rehearsal. For a session with no consent sheet, or with a sheet whose scope is unclear, tell staff not to publish a link and to refer it to the archive coordinator. Where permission only covers selected tracks, don't extend it to the rest of the session. If a file has passed its checksum check but permission is still unclear, the archive must keep it out of public access until the coordinator clarifies the consent. Make that condition easy to find later in the guide, not just a note buried next to file copying. Don't claim that the coordinator has approved anything in this example.

The guide should mention a few ordinary details that matter on shift: some transfers arrive on memory cards, but staff must not erase or return one until its contents have been checked and the intake log has been updated; headphones are kept in the top drawer at Rowan; and the hall's label printer sometimes produces faint text, so a volunteer should compare a printed label with the session log before attaching it to a box. Boxes should be lifted by two people when full. If a box is damp or smells strongly of mould, stop handling it and tell the staff member on duty; don't put it on the new shelves. That is a precaution for a possible problem, not a claim that the collection currently has mould or damp boxes.

Use short headings and numbered steps where they help. Include a compact section called “Before leaving the intake desk” that reminds the volunteer to put the paper log back in the correct year folder, record where the box was placed, return the headphones to the top drawer, and report any unresolved checksum mismatch to the archive coordinator. Also remind them not to make a public link if consent is unclear. Keep the voice calm and practical, and use “staff” for paid workers and “volunteer” where a step can be done by the rotating volunteers. Please avoid implying that volunteers can decide consent questions or authorize public access. The guide should distinguish an unresolved issue from a completed check, and it should not fill in missing session details or invent a resolution for a flagged item.

Please make the resulting guide suitable for printing as a few pages beside the intake desk. It can explain the workflow in enough detail for a new volunteer to follow, but don't add a glossary, a sample completed log, a new retention schedule or a recommendation to replace the current system. End with a substantive reminder about checking both file integrity and access permission as separate matters, while keeping the unresolved cases with the coordinator. The last paragraph should not imply that all 640 sessions have been processed or that the storage move is finished.", "output": "Create a practical internal guide for the North Quay Rehearsal Archive explaining how staff and volunteers handle rehearsal recordings from arrival through an access decision. This is an operational guide, not an archive history, broad policy, or legal document. Write in plain, calm language for two part-time staff members and rotating volunteers, so the steps can be followed during an intake shift. Make the guide suitable for printing as a few pages beside the intake desk.

## Context

The North Quay Rehearsal Archive is a small nonprofit collection in a converted community hall. It holds about 640 sessions recorded by local theatre and dance groups between 2014 and 2022. Most recordings are WAV audio, with a smaller number of MP3s and a few rehearsal videos. Some sessions have only a paper session log; others also have a consent sheet and a typed set list.

The team is preparing a new storage area after a leak in the old cupboard. The recordings were not exposed to water. About 80 boxes are moving to shelves in room 2B; do not imply that any audio was damaged or that the move is complete. The intake-desk computer is called Rowan, and the separate backup drive is named Birch. The current file-naming pattern uses the session date, group name, and a short sequence number, as in `20190514_CopperKite_02.wav`. There is no database. Paper logs are kept in folders by year, and staff currently write the intake date and box or shelf location on each log. Suggest a consistent order for the steps, but do not propose buying equipment or software.

## Intake and copying workflow

Present the following steps in a usable sequence, distinguishing what staff check from what they record:

1. Receive the box or transfer and compare its contents with the paper session log.
2. Note missing, duplicated, or unreadable items. Do not guess what a missing recording contained.
3. Briefly check a file's playback for obvious corruption. Staff are not expected to listen to the whole rehearsal.
4. Record the date received and the physical box or shelf location on the paper log.
5. Copy digital files to Rowan and Birch, then use the archive's checksum tool to verify the copies against the source.
6. Keep consent sheets with the relevant year's paper folders, not inside boxes with audio carriers.

Do not treat a file that opens as automatically cleared for public listening. Checksum verification establishes whether a copy matches its source; it does not determine consent or sound quality. Do not suggest that a paper log contains details that were never written on it.

Make the copying action conditional and show both branches clearly:

- If the checksum matches the source, keep the source file unchanged and retain the verified copies on Rowan and Birch.
- If the checksum does not match, do not replace or overwrite the source. Set the suspect copy aside and notify the archive coordinator before anyone tries another copy. This branch applies to the affected file and does not mean that every file in the box failed. The coordinator's next decision is outside the scope of this guide; do not invent what happens after notification.

Repeat this rule in the section on closing an intake shift, so it remains visible after the copying steps.

## Access and consent

Keep access decisions separate from file checks. Some groups permitted staff-only preservation but have not agreed to public listening. Other groups signed consent sheets allowing public access to selected sessions; a sheet may cover specific tracks or set-list items rather than an entire rehearsal.

For a session with no consent sheet, or with a sheet whose scope is unclear, instruct staff not to publish a link and to refer the matter to the archive coordinator. If permission covers only selected tracks, do not extend it to the rest of the session. If a file passes its checksum check but permission remains unclear, keep it out of public access until the coordinator clarifies the consent. Make this condition easy to find later in the guide, not just a note beside the copying instructions. Do not claim that the coordinator has approved anything in this example, and do not imply that volunteers can decide consent questions or authorize public access.

## Other shift details

Include these practical details:

- Some transfers arrive on memory cards. Staff must not erase or return a card until its contents have been checked and the intake log updated.
- Headphones are kept in the top drawer at Rowan.
- The hall's label printer sometimes produces faint text. Before attaching a printed label to a box, the volunteer should compare it with the session log.
- Two people should lift a box when it is full.
- If a box is damp or smells strongly of mould, stop handling it and tell the staff member on duty; do not put it on the new shelves. Present this as a precaution for a possible problem, not as a claim that the collection currently has mould or damp boxes.

## Before leaving the intake desk

Include a compact section with a reminder to return the paper log to the correct year folder, record where the box was placed, return the headphones to Rowan's top drawer, and report any unresolved checksum mismatch to the archive coordinator. Remind volunteers not to make a public link when consent is unclear. Distinguish unresolved issues from completed checks, and do not fill in missing session details or invent a resolution for a flagged item.

Use short headings and numbered steps where helpful. Use “staff” for paid workers and “volunteer” where a step can be done by the rotating volunteers. Explain the workflow in enough detail for a new volunteer to follow, but do not add a glossary, sample completed log, new retention schedule, or recommendation to replace the current system. End with a substantive reminder that file integrity and access permission are separate matters and that unresolved cases stay with the coordinator. Do not imply that all 640 sessions have been processed or that the storage move is finished."}]
